paragraphs.text: Why banks depend on one hidden network.

Most people never see it. In 2015 SWIFT linked more than 11,000 financial institutions in over 200 countries and territories. Its members were exchanging an average of over 32 million messages per day. As of 2018, around half of all high-value cross-border payments worldwide used the SWIFT network. SWIFT is a cooperative established in 1973 in Belgium and owned by its member banks and firms. SWIFT does not manage accounts for individuals or institutions and does not hold funds from third parties. SWIFT was founded in Brussels on 3 May 1973. It was initially supported by 239 banks in 15 countries. After a payment is initiated, it must be settled through a payment system such as T2 in Europe. SWIFT assigns ISO 9362 Business Identifier Codes, popularly known as SWIFT codes. Cross-border bank payments depend on standardised SWIFT messages between institutions.
Here is how it works. Banks exchange standardised payment instructions over SWIFT; settlement itself happens through accounts held elsewhere.
That is the bottleneck. Replacing it means every counterparty adopting another messaging system, identifier scheme and security setup at once.
The failure would not stay contained. A bank cut off from the network can still hold money but struggles to instruct payments abroad, isolating its customers.
So what protects the system? Alternative domestic messaging systems, correspondent workarounds and contingency channels exist but cover only part of the traffic.
